title: A first private message is I/O-sensitive by 30x: find its write and fsync count
description:
`private_queries_are_one_to_one_rooms` (crates/mimid-agent/tests/irc_v2.rs)
ran 349.61s, 375.65s and 11.77s on the same code. The two slow runs
followed a `cargo clean`: cold page cache, a full rebuild competing for
the disk, and 178 GiB freed on the filesystem underneath. The fast run
was a warm build with nothing competing. So the path is not slow; it is
I/O-sensitive by three orders of magnitude, which is the same thing to
a user on a loaded phone.

## What to find

What a first private message does between the `PRIVMSG` and the line
coming back. The pieces, from the crate map: `Store::action` creates the
one-to-one room, the agent fetches a KeyPackage, creates the MLS group,
sends a Welcome, and `Store::sync` reads the journal back. Each of those
touches `mimid.sqlite` and OpenMLS's state in the same database.

The question to answer with numbers, not reading: how many write
transactions and how many fsyncs does one private query cost? A path
that commits per MLS operation rather than per user action multiplies
every disk stall by that count, and that multiplier is what turns 11s
into 350s.

## Method

Depends on bead mimid-604m.1 (the daemon logs nothing). With a
subscriber installed, a span per step and `sqlx`'s slow-statement
warning already at 1s, one slow run names the step. Reproduce the
pressure deliberately rather than waiting for another `cargo clean`:
run the test while a second process writes to the same filesystem.

## Not a fix for the test

The test is correct and its wait has no deadline any more, so it
measures rather than fails. Do not make it wait differently.
notes:
2026-11-27 07:30: the pressure is identified. load average 80.55 on 18 cores, with 81 cargo-mutants processes running a mutation campaign on PKIX out of /data/tmp/cargo-mutants-PKIX-*. That is what both slow runs (349.61s, 375.65s) and the 2.4s PRAGMA were measured under, and it is still running: mimid-agent-core's own lib unit tests (frank::tests, agent::didwebvh_tests, which no sweep touched) each take over 60 seconds right now against seconds when the machine is idle. So the 30x figure in this bead's title is a measurement under a 4.5x CPU oversubscription, not a property of the first-DM path alone. Re-measure deliberately: run the test alone, then again under a known load, rather than waiting to be surprised. The bug in mimid-604m still stands -- the agent says nothing while it waits -- and bead mimid-604m.1 is what makes the next measurement readable.
Measured 2026-11-27 in a worktree at a932ec4b. One first private
message over IRC: PRIVMSG to a nick no room exists for, which is
Store::open_direct then Store::send_message. One in-process provider,
two daemons, sync_interval_ms = 100, both state directories and the
provider's database on one filesystem. Hops read back in process with
mimid_telemetry::timeline, as tests/message_path.rs does; writes and
fsyncs counted with strace -f -y -T -ttt around the test binary, the
window bounded by an unlink of a unique path either side of the PRIVMSG.

## The counts the bead asked for

Sender's mimid.sqlite: 36 committed write transactions, 35 of them
before the echo. 145 fsyncs: 73 on mimid.sqlite-journal, 36 on
mimid.sqlite, 36 on the directory. And 36 journal files created and
unlinked.
Receiver's mimid.sqlite: 12 transactions, 47 fsyncs (23 + 12 + 12).
The provider's a.example.sqlite: 19 fsyncs, every one on the -wal, no
directory fsync, no unlink.

48 write transactions and 192 fsyncs on the two agent databases for one
first private message: four fsyncs per commit, because the agent's
database is in SQLite's default rollback-journal mode while
mimid-server's store sets journal_mode = WAL (store/mod.rs:133).
PRAGMA journal_mode on the agent's database reads "delete".

The journalling mode, not the transaction count, is the larger half of
the multiplier -- and it cannot be changed without a decision. See bead
mimid-604m.5: a log takes 192 fsyncs to 49 and 35.8 s to 11.2 s, and
breaks a_destroyed_chat_takes_its_messages_bans_and_attachments
(mimid-agent-jmap tests/chat_delete.rs:528), which reads the raw
mimid.sqlite and requires a destroyed chat's text not to be in it,
because secure_delete's overwrite then reaches the file at the next
checkpoint rather than at the commit. Measured, then reverted; the four
choices are in that bead, labelled human.

## Which hop dominates: not the send, the room

                                    idle-ish    under pressure
  PRIVMSG to store_send opening      1.09 s        21.2 s
  store_send, whole                  0.19 s        12.8 s
    agent_send_content               0.09 s         5.3 s
      mls_encrypt_and_stage          0.02 s         0.48 s
      provider_submit                0.04 s         1.54 s
  echo at the client                 1.39 s        35.8 s

The gap before store_send is Store::open_direct -> Agent::host_room +
Agent::invite: the MLS group, the first Commit, the Welcome, and every
transaction they commit. It had no span, so 78% of a first private
message was invisible to the timeline bead mimid-604m.1 added. The
periodic sync shows it from the other side: alice's store_sync span
opened 1.5 ms after the PRIVMSG and its own agent_receive child only
1088 ms later, which is how long it waited for the agent mutex the room
creation held.

Fixed here: store_host_room over Store::host, with agent_host_room and
agent_invite under it. The hop now reads

  store_host_room   429.7 ms   (agent_host_room 230.1, agent_invite 199.2)
  store_send        204.1 ms   (agent_send_content 51.7)

so two thirds of a first private message is the room, and says so.

## Answered along the way

No KeyPackage fetch is inside a transaction, and none can be:
Agent::in_transaction takes a synchronous closure ("step is synchronous,
so no transaction is [held across an await]", agent.rs), so no network
call is ever inside one. The bead's third hypothesis is ruled out by
construction, not by measurement.

An idle sync costs no fsync either: Database::save_with opens an
IMMEDIATE transaction every time, but a transaction that dirties no page
commits without touching the disk. The 100 ms poll is not the I/O.

## The pressure, deliberately

strace -f on a machine at load average 46 over 18 cores was enough:
mean fsync 279 ms, longest 1.78 s, against roughly 7 ms with nothing in
the way. The same first DM went 1.39 s to 35.8 s. 192 fsyncs is the
multiplier that does it. The 30x in this bead's title is reproducible on
demand and needs no cargo clean.

## What is left

1. Bead mimid-604m.5, the journalling mode, which is Mark's to decide.
2. 36 write transactions for one user action, untouched. Each is an MLS
step -- the group, a proposal, the Commit, the outbox entry, the hub's
answer, each received Message -- and they are the crash cut points the
outbox is built on, so merging them is a durability change rather than a
refactor.
3. Bead mimid-604m.3's premise that journal_mode is per connection holds
for sqlx's pool only: the mode lives in the database file's header, so a
second connection to a database already in WAL inherits it, and the
pragma is then the no-op that still takes the write lock, which is the
cost that bead describes.
close_reason: Counted: 36 write transactions and 145 fsyncs on the sender's mimid.sqlite, 12 and 47 on the receiver's, for one first private message; four fsyncs a commit, because the agent's database is in SQLite's default rollback-journal mode. The dominant hop is the room, not the send, and it now has spans (commit c1c8e1ce). The mode cannot be changed without trading secure_delete's promptness: bead mimid-604m.5, labelled human.
